newsitem.title: ITALY: France, Germany push for EU defence policy.
newsitem.headline: France, Germany push for EU defence policy.

text.p: France, Italy and Germany called on Tuesday for the creation of a common European Union defence structure and policy, but they faced a wall of opposition from the bloc's keenest Atlanticists as well as its neutrals.

At the 40th anniversary of the EU's founding Treaty of Rome, the three countries, supported by Spain, Belgium and Luxembourg, said the Western European Union (WEU) defence grouping should be gradually but fully incorporated into the EU.
This should take place in three phases, they said, with no dates as yet proposed.
First, WEU procedures and structures would be linked with those of the EU while retaining the independence of the defence grouping.
The second phase would see the EU take over decision-making for the WEU, initiating military actions where called for.
Finally, the WEU would be brought fully into the Union, allowing unwilling member states to stay out of actions they oppose.
The result would be to give the EU a common defence policy, something sought by the bloc's keenest integrationists since the earliest days of its development.
Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said the plan would help "give concrete shape to a European defence and security identity".

Ten EU countries are currently in the WEU, which has no military arm but which under a new arrangement will be able to borrow NATO equipment and command structures to conduct humanitarian and peace-keeping missions.

Diplomats said the move appeared to be an attempt by the EU's core countries to inject some political momentum into the bloc's inter-governmental conference (IGC), the rewriting of its treaty due to end in June in Amsterdam.
But many pronounced the idea stillborn because of vehement opposition from Britain as well as the bloc's neutrals, any of which could decide to veto it.
"It sinks before its swims," one diplomat from a neutral country said.

British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind repeated his country's objections, saying that turning the EU into a defence body would make relations with Russia more difficult and threatened the bloc's planned enlargement into eastern Europe.
"It is not part of the benefit of the (NATO) Atlantic Alliance to turn the European Union into an organisation for collective security," Rifkind said.

Although Britain's ruling Conservative party is widely exepected to be out of office by the time IGC is completed -- defeated in a May 1 election -- the opposition Labour party is also against incorporation of the WEU into the EU.
NATO members Denmark and to a lesser extent Portugal also oppose the plan as do the EU's neutral countries -- Ireland, Sweden, Finland and Austria.
